text: ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation.

text: In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is \beginarray r \triangle E = E _ LUMO - E _ HOMO = 3.3 0 2 ~ eV, \endarray indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes.

text: Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips. 1 As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes, 2,3 necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu. 4 However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers. 5 Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.

text: 6 The deposition quality of chip interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of the chip, directly afecting the chip’s yield, reliability, and stability. This places higher demands on the chip interconnect process. Electroplating technology is the primary technique for forming micro and nano interconnect structures. 7 In this complex process, additives play a critical role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metals. 8 Similar to the traditional Damascene copper interconnect process, the cobalt interconnect plating system also requires additives that can increase the metal deposition overpotential to achieve void-free superfilling in micro and nano structures. 9 The cobalt superfilling additives reported to date often contain unsaturated carbon bonds, nitrogencontaining functional groups, or a combination of both. The nitrogen-containing functional groups exist in the forms of amines ( - NH _2, \Gamma - NH), oxime groups ( - C=N-OH) and nitrogen-containing heterocycles. text: 3.1.2. Cathodic Polarization Curve. Linear scanning voltammetry (LSV) was used to evaluate the inhibitory efect of the inhibitor (5-EP) on the cobalt deposition process. The evaluation was carried out at two diferent rotational speeds: 2000 and 200 rpm. The relevant results are shown in Figure 2. With the addition of 5-EP, it can be noticed that the overpotential increases, and the additive adsorbs on the surface of the electrode, forming a film of material that causes the electrochemical reaction to take place on this film rather than on the electrode surface. In this case, the additives may occupy the active sites on the electrode surface, leading to a negative potential shift. 24,25 Regardless of the rotational speed setting, it is found that the addition of 5-EP leads to a steady shift of the reduction potential in a negative direction. This suggests that the inhibitor (5-EP) increases the cathodic polarization and prevents the reduction of Co ^2 + at the cathode. In addition, the ability of 5-EP to inhibit cobalt deposition was significantly higher at high speeds than at low speeds.

text: 3.3. Theoretical Calculations and Simulations. 3.3.1. Quantum Chemical Calculations. Quantum chemical calculations were employed to elucidate the adsorption process of the inhibitor (5-EP) and to predict its potential adsorption sites. The molecule was inserted into a Gaussian function for structural optimization and computation. The resulting data were then visualized using Multiwfn and VMD software. 27,28 In accordance with the frontier molecular orbital theory, the energy levels of the HOMO and the LUMO play a crucial role in determining chemical reactions. 29 The HOMO energy ( E _ HOMO) reflects the molecule’s inclination to give away electrons, whereas the LUMO energy ( E _ LUMO) reflects its inclination to receive electrons. A larger E _ HOMO value implies a greater capacity of the molecule to donate electrons, while a lower E _ LUMO value suggests a better ability to accept electron s. 30,31 The computational results are depicted in Figure Sa, b..
section: Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors > 3. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

text: The figure shows that the electron cloud density in the HOMO state is basically distributed over the entire molecular structure of 5-EP, while in the LUMO state, the electron cloud density is mainly distributed on the pyrimidine ring. According to the calculations, E _ LUMO = - 3.9 0 6 ~ eV, E _ HOMO = - 6.9 3 8 ~ eV, and the energy gap \triangle E = E _ LUMO - E _ HOMO = 3.3 0 2 ~ eV.~A smaller \triangle E denotes greater reactivity of the chemical. The extremely small energy diference ( \triangle E) between the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital ( E _ LUMO) and the highest occupied molecular orbital ( E _ HOMO) suggests that the additive molecules have a strong tendency to absorb and donate electrons at the electrode surface. The value of \triangle E is directly related to the adsorption intensity of the additive molecules on the metal interface. A smaller \bigtriangleup E value indicates a higher adsorption strength of the molecules at the metal interface, leading to stronger inhibitory efects on cobalt electro deposition.

As shown in Figure 5c, the ESP calculation results can represent the electron density contributions of the groups, identifying potential chemical reaction sites. The ESP values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values indicate higher electron density. Therefore, the electron density distribution of 5-EP suggests that the acetylene group ( - C \equiv C -) with its high electron density is a potential site for adsorption during cobalt electrodeposition. In summary, the 5-EP molecule, with its acetylene group ( - C \equiv. C−), can efectively adsorb onto cobalt, thereby inhibiting the process of cobalt electrodeposition.

text: 3.3.2. MD Simulation. Furthermore, we performed MD simulations using the Materials Studio software to examine the adsorption properties of the 5-EP molecule on the cobalt metal surface. The simulation results, illustrated in Figure ^ 6, demonstrate that the 5-EP molecule adsorbs parallelly on the Co(100) surface. This adsorption behavior aligns with the findings of quantum chemical analysis. The aforementioned ESP study indicates that lower ESP values correspond to higher electron density. In the 5-EP molecule, regions of high electron density are mainly located at the alkyne group ( - C \equiv C−) and the functional groups on the pyrimidine ring (−N− C�C−). Due to the efect of these functional groups, the 5- EP molecule can adsorb parallelly onto the cobalt metal surface. The adsorption energy of the molecule on the Co(100) surface was calculated using the equation E = E _ total - E _ Co - E _ 5-EP, ^ 3 2, 3 3 yielding a value of −133.96 kcal/ mol. This negative adsorption energy indicates a favorable and strong adsorption capacity of the 5-EP molecule, which is consistent with its ability to inhibit cobalt electrodeposition.

text: 3.4. Blind Hole Filling Experiment. Based on the electrochemical experimental findings, it is anticipated that the inclusion of additives would enhance the electroplating and filling of cobalt in blind holes. Therefore, an experiment was conducted to examine the impact of the inhibitor molecule (5- EP) on blind hole filling with cobalt. Figure 7 illustrates the cross-sectional images of blind hole filled cobalt deposited at various time intervals. As depicted in Figure 7a, when 6 ppm of 5-EP was added to the electrolyte for electroplating, a Vshaped filling of cobalt deposition in the blind hole was observed after 3 h, due to convection and mass transfer efects. Figure 7b shows that with increased electroplating time, the cobalt layer in the blind hole exhibited a bottom-up filling trend, although superfilling was not yet achieved. As shown in Figure 7c, after 5 h of electroplating, the blind hole was completely filled without voids or gaps. This indicates that 5- EP initially adsorbs at the mouth of the blind hole during the electroplating process, inhibiting cobalt deposition at the entrance.

text: 3.5. Characterization. 3.5.1. SEM/AFM Characterization. The surface morphology of the cobalt deposited from the electrolyte with diferent concentrations of the inhibitor (5- EP) was analyzed using SEM. The relevant SEM data are displayed in Figure 9. Figure 9a clearly shows that the cobalt coating obtained from the electroplating solution with additives has a rough and porous surface, characterized by the presence of massive growth clusters. The presence of the inhibitor (5-EP) clearly alters the micro morphology of the cobalt coating. As shown in Figure 8b−d, introducing an inhibitor (5-EP) can efectively improve the quality of the cobalt layer. When 2 ppm of inhibitor (5-EP) was added, the cobalt particle size decreased. When the concentration of inhibitor (5-EP) was increased to 4 ppm, the cobalt particle size was further reduced, and the surface of the plated layer was smooth. When the inhibitor (5-EP) is added up to 6 ppm, the cobalt grain size on the coated surface is minimized, and the coating is smooth and flat in the macroscopic state.

text: 3.5.4. Contact Angle Test. The wettability of the electrolyte to the electrode is an important parameter during electro deposition. Here the surface contact angle meter (Kruss K100- MK2) was used to measure the contact angle value of the plating solution containing a leveling agent on the surface of the plated layer after diferent plating times. The PCB boards with plating times of 1−5 h were prepared in advance and cleaned with deionized water, and 5μL droplets were dropped on their surfaces during the test and the images were instantly stored for measurement. Figure 13 shows the contact angle (CA) value of the droplets on the PCB with diferent deposition times. As shown in Figure 13, the contact angle of the blank control sample is greater than 30°, and with the increase of deposition time, the contact angle gradually becomes smaller, respectively, 76.1, 52.8, 34.4, 20.7, and 5.6 ^°.. The small value of CA indicates that the interfacial energy between the electrolyte and the surface of the plated layer is higher, and the easier it is to be wetted.

text: 4. CONCLUSIONS
section: Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors > 4. CONCLUSIONS

text: In summary, this study employs 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry (CV) and LSV reveal that 5-EP efectively suppresses the reduction of Co ^2 +. Additionally, electrochemical tests indicate the significant role of the ethynyl functional group ( - C \equiv C -) in the cobalt electrodeposition process. Further studies on the impact of 5-EP on cobalt nucleation showed that in th absence of 5-EP, cobalt nucleation occurred through a three dimensional instantaneous process, whereas the addition of 5- EP shifted the nucleation to a three-dimensional progressive process. 5-EP efectively reduced the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and promoted the growth of cobalt grains in the directions of Co(100) and Co(110). The resistivity of the cobalt coating remained essentially at 10 μΩ·cm. According to quantum chemical calculations and MD simulations, it was discovered that 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5-EP), which contains an ethynyl group ( - C \equiv C -), can efectively adsorb onto cobalt The adsorption energy of 5-EP was calculated to be −133.96 kcal/mol on the Co(100) surface, indicating its strong adsorption capability.
section: Study of 5‑Alkynylpyrimidines as Cobalt Superfilling Inhibitors > 4. CONCLUSIONS

text: Electroplating experiments showed that adding 6 ppm of 5-EP to the plating solution and electroplating for 5 h resulted in defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, in situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy was employed to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. By observing in situ enhanced Raman spectra at different potentials. it was found that as the potential stepped, the peak intensities at 1092cm^-1 (ring vibration, C−H in-plane deformation shear vibration), 1414 cm^-1 (pyrimidine ring skeleton N = C = N plane bending vibration), 1573 cm −1 (overall bending vibration of the pyrimidine ring skeleton), and 2125~cm^-1 (carbon−carbon triple bond ( C \equiv C) stretching vibration) increased. This indicates that during the electroplating process, the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules primarily adsorb onto the cobalt layer surface through these functional groups, thereby inhibiting the deposition of cobalt.

text: The contact angle test showed that the contact angle of the plated surface decreased from 99.7 to 5.6 ^° with the increase in deposition time, and the inhibitor (5-EP) significantly improved the wettability of the plating solution which helped to improve the quality of the plated layer. This can indicate the efectiveness of using 5-ethynylpyrimidine (5- EP) as a single inhibitor for cobalt electrodeposition.
